messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tailor
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma, Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi sits in the therapy room with his back pressed firmly against the wall, his chair angled so he has an unobstructed view of the door. At 33, his tailor’s hands, usually steady and precise, rest restlessly in his lap. It has been fourteen months since the attack at the community market, and the life he knew has unraveled thread by thread. He had been there selecting fabrics for a client, enjoying the Saturday morning bustle, when the world dissolved into a deafening roar and a cloud of white dust. He remembers the split second before—the vibrant colors of an Ankara print—and the moments after, scrambling over debris. But the instant of the blast itself, and the minutes that followed, are a complete blank, a hole in his memory he can’t patch no matter how hard he tries.

In the aftermath, the memories that did remain began to play on a loop. While hunched over his sewing machine, the whir of the motor would suddenly be drowned out by the phantom sound of screaming, the image of scattered produce and overturned stalls flashing behind his eyes. It is like a film, he says, one he’s forced to watch over and over. Other times, a strange and unsettling numbness descends. He can recount the facts of that day—where he was standing, what he was wearing—with the detached calm of a news reporter, as if describing something that happened to a stranger he once knew. The emotional disconnect is terrifying in its own way, making him feel alien in his own skin. He has come to believe he is a weak person; the man who survived is not strong, but a hollowed-out version of who he used to be.

This conviction now dictates his every move. His small tailor shop, once a place of pride and creativity, has become a fortress. He rearranged the entire layout so that his cutting table and sewing station face the entrance, ensuring no one can enter without him seeing them first. He feels a profound sense of unease unless his back is against a solid surface. When he must visit his fabric supplier downtown, the trip is an ordeal. Upon entering the warehouse, he doesn't see the bolts of silk and cotton; he sees a map of potential threats and escape routes, his mind automatically cataloging every exit. This constant state of being on guard is exhausting, leaving him drained before his workday has even truly begun.

Over the months, he has developed ways to quiet his mind, but they have come at a cost. He can lose entire nights to scrolling on his phone or playing mindless games, anything to create a wall of digital noise that keeps the "film" from starting. He has also found a strange, temporary relief in conflict. He will pick arguments with his landlord over trivial maintenance issues or escalate a simple disagreement with a customer into a heated confrontation. The surge of adrenaline from the argument provides a momentary distraction, a different kind of danger that feels more manageable than the one replaying in his head. But the relief is fleeting, always replaced by shame and a deepening sense of isolation. He feels he no longer belongs anywhere, least of all among the friends from his community who also survived. He is certain they can see the weakness in him, the man who froze, the man who can’t hold himself together.

He avoids making any plans more than a day or two in advance. The thought of a future—a wedding suit to be made in six months, a holiday to plan for—fills him with a paralyzing dread. He can’t trust that he will do the right thing, that he will be able to follow through, that he will even be the same person by then. It was this fear that finally brought him to seek help. A long-term client, whose family he had been outfitting for years, asked him to design the suits for his son’s wedding next fall. Kofi found himself unable to commit, making excuses until the client, frustrated and confused by his behavior, took his business elsewhere. The loss of the commission was a significant financial blow, but the loss of the relationship felt like a final confirmation of his own failure. He is here now because he is terrified that this is all he will ever be: a man perpetually scanning for exits from a life he no longer knows how to live.
